title: Leader election with leases and fencing tokens
description: Three nodes compete for a TTL lease via compare-and-swap; the leader renews, a paused leader loses the lease, and fencing tokens reject its late write.
outcome: You can elect a leader with a TTL lease and CAS, reason about failover time, and protect a resource with fencing tokens.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: etcd v3.7.3 container + etcdctl (pending-ci).
overview: A lease is a lock with an expiry; it gives automatic failover but cannot stop a paused ex-leader, so the resource must check a fencing token that only grows.

glossary.meaning: Ownership of a key that expires after a TTL unless renewed.
Write only if the key is still at the revision you expect; otherwise fail.
A number that grows with every new lease holder; the resource rejects lower ones.

concepts: Acquire = CAS create-if-absent; renew = CAS on your own revision.
Only the resource can stop a paused ex-leader: check fencing tokens there.

code:
"""L200 lesson 7 (python election.py): three nodes compete for a lease in a shared KV store (TTL +
compare-and-swap). The leader renews every tick; when it pauses, the lease expires, another node takes
over with a HIGHER fencing token, and storage rejects the old leader's late write. Simulated clock."""
from helpers import SimClock, call, serve
from kv_store import KVStore

KEY, TTL = "leader", 3.0  # lease TTL 3 s; nodes act once per 1 s tick, so the leader renews at TTL/3


class Node:
    def __init__(self, name, url):
        self.name, self.url, self.rev, self.token, self.paused = name, url, 0, None, False

    def pause(self):  # e.g. a long GC pause: the node stops acting but still BELIEVES it leads
        self.paused = True

    def resume(self):
        self.paused = False

    def step(self, t, storage, log):
        if self.paused:
            return
        if self.token is not None:  # I think I am the leader: do the work, then renew
            log(f"t={t} {self.name} writes with token {self.token}: {storage.write(self.token, f'{self.name}@t{t}')}")
            status, body, _ = call(self.url + "/cas", {"key": KEY, "expect": self.rev, "value": self.name, "ttl": TTL})
            if status == 200:
                self.rev = body["rev"]  # renewed: CAS on MY revision, TTL restarts
            else:
                log(f"t={t} {self.name} renew failed (rev {self.rev} != {body['rev']}) -> steps down")
                self.token = None
            return
        status, _, _ = call(self.url + "/get", {"key": KEY})
        if status == 404:  # lease free (never taken, or expired): try to create it, expect rev 0
            status, body, _ = call(self.url + "/cas", {"key": KEY, "expect": 0, "value": self.name, "ttl": TTL})
            if status == 200:  # only one CAS can win; the losers see 409
                self.rev, self.token = body["rev"], body["created"]  # fencing token = creation revision
                log(f"t={t} {self.name} acquired the lease, fencing token {self.token}")


class FencedStorage:
    """The protected resource: rejects a write whose token is lower than the highest it has seen."""
    def __init__(self, fencing=True):
        self.fencing, self.max_token, self.value = fencing, 0, None

    def write(self, token, value):
        if self.fencing and token < self.max_token:
            return f"REJECTED (token {token} < {self.max_token})"
        self.max_token, self.value = max(self.max_token, token), value
        return "accepted"


def simulate(ticks=9, events=None, fencing=True, quiet=False):
    """events: {tick: (node_name, method_name)}. Returns {'log', 'holders', 'storage'}."""
    clock, lines, holders = SimClock(), [], []
    KVStore.reset(clock)
    srv = serve(KVStore)
    url, storage = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_port}", FencedStorage(fencing)
    nodes = {n: Node(n, url) for n in ("n1", "n2", "n3")}
    log = lines.append if quiet else (lambda s: (lines.append(s), print(s)))
    for t in range(ticks):
        if t in (events or {}):
            name, action = events[t]
            getattr(nodes[name], action)()  # the lab's events: pause / resume (build task: resign)
            log(f"t={t} {name} {action}")
        for node in nodes.values():  # fixed order n1, n2, n3 -> deterministic
            node.step(t, storage, log)
        status, body, _ = call(url + "/get", {"key": KEY})
        holders.append((t, body.get("value"), body.get("created")) if status == 200 else (t, None, None))
        clock.advance(1.0)
    srv.shutdown()
    srv.server_close()
    return {"log": lines, "holders": holders, "storage": storage}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = simulate(events={3: ("n1", "pause"), 7: ("n1", "resume")})
    print("lease holder per tick:", " ".join(f"{t}:{h or '-'}" for t, h, _ in out["holders"]))
    print("storage value:", out["storage"].value, "| highest token seen:", out["storage"].max_token)

codeWalkthrough.title: CAS create-if-absent
codeWalkthrough.detail: `call(url + "/cas", {"key": KEY, "expect": 0, ...})` succeeds for exactly one node; `body["created"]` (the creation revision) becomes the fencing token.

codeWalkthrough.title: Renew on my revision
codeWalkthrough.detail: The leader sends `expect: self.rev`; if another node created the key since, the revisions differ, the store answers 409 and the node steps down.

codeWalkthrough.title: Work before renew
codeWalkthrough.detail: `step()` writes first, then renews. That is why the woken n1 still writes at t=7: it only learns it lost the lease afterwards — exactly the gap fencing closes.

codeWalkthrough.title: Fenced storage
codeWalkthrough.detail: `FencedStorage.write` rejects `token < max_token`; it is the only place that can make a stale leader harmless.

troubleshooting.symptom: Two nodes both think they lead
troubleshooting.action: Expected during a pause; make the resource check fencing tokens.
Shorten the TTL (renew more often) or add resign() on clean shutdown.

equivalents: Same idea in etcd: `etcdctl lease grant`, `txn` with `create("leader") = "0"` (CAS) and the key's `create_revision` as fencing token; `etcdctl elect` = the election API (`/v3/election/campaign`).
Same idea in Kubernetes: Lease objects (coordination.k8s.io) for kube-controller-manager / kube-scheduler leader election.
Same idea in ZooKeeper: the zxid or znode version as fencing token.
Valkey `SET lock me NX EX 30` is a lease without a fencing token: fine for efficiency, not for correctness.
inRealSystems: Kubernetes control-plane components elect one active instance with Lease objects; an alpha feature releases the lock on exit instead of waiting for the TTL.
etcd leases delete attached keys when the TTL elapses; `etcdctl elect` resigns on SIGTERM.
HBase once had the paused-leader bug that fencing tokens prevent.
useWhen: Use a lease when exactly one worker may own a job or shard and the store offers atomic CAS + TTL; add fencing whenever correctness (not just efficiency) depends on it; avoid when every replica could safely do the work.
simulatorVsReal: One process, simulated clock: pauses are an event, not a real GC stop; the store is in-memory, not replicated (etcd uses Raft for that).
caution: A lease never guarantees a single actor by itself: clocks, pauses and network delays can exceed the TTL. Protect every write with a fencing token.

conceptSummary: A lease is ownership with an expiry, taken and renewed with compare-and-swap; failover happens when the TTL runs out. A paused ex-leader cannot know it lost the lease, so the protected resource rejects writes whose fencing token is lower than one it has seen.

title: At-least-once messaging: ack, visibility timeout, redelivery, dead letters
description: A tiny HTTP broker hides received messages for a visibility timeout, redelivers unacked ones, and dead-letters poison; crashing consumers create duplicate charges.
outcome: You can explain and configure ack, visibility timeout and dead-lettering, and make a consumer idempotent so redelivery is harmless.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps).
overview: Brokers redeliver anything not acked, so nothing is lost but work can run twice; consumers must be idempotent and poison messages must be parked.

glossary.meaning: How long a received message stays hidden before it is redelivered unless acked.
The consumer's 'done': the broker deletes the message.
Where messages go after too many failed deliveries.
A message that makes the handler fail every time.

concepts: Receive hides; ack deletes; no ack = redelivery.
Bound redeliveries with a DLQ; make consumers idempotent.

title: Sharding with consistent hashing: virtual nodes, key movement, hot keys
description: A hash ring with 100 virtual nodes per node; measure keys moved when a node joins or leaves (vs hash % N), load balance, and a hot key.
outcome: You can place keys on a hash ring, predict how many move on membership changes, choose vnode counts, and place replicas on distinct nodes.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional agent assist: Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible local server (tests use the fake server only).
overview: Consistent hashing moves about 1/N of the keys when a node joins or leaves, instead of almost all of them; virtual nodes keep the load even, but no hash fixes a hot key.

glossary.meaning: Hash values arranged in a circle; a key belongs to the next node point clockwise.
One of many ring positions owned by the same physical node.
A single key that receives a large share of all requests.

concepts: hash % N reshuffles ~80% of keys going from 4 to 5 nodes; a ring ~20%.
Replicas = keep walking clockwise to N distinct nodes.

equivalents: Same idea in Apache Cassandra: a token ring with multiple tokens per node (vnodes); replicas found by walking the ring to distinct nodes (SimpleStrategy).
Same idea in memcache clients (Facebook's memcache paper): items spread over servers by consistent hashing.
Amazon Dynamo (the paper) introduced virtual nodes for this balance problem.
inRealSystems: Cassandra maps every node to one or more tokens; 2.x used 256 random tokens per node, 3.x+ a deterministic allocator needing fewer.
Facebook's memcache uses consistent hashing and notes a single key can take 20% of a server's requests.
useWhen: Use consistent hashing when nodes join and leave and moving data is expensive; avoid it for a fixed node set (modulo is simpler) or when you need ordered range scans.
caution: Agent assist: the model only proposes a layout; check() decides and a rejected layout is never applied. Do not put hostnames, credentials or customer keys in prompts.

code:
"""L200 lesson 10 (python cache.py): cache-aside with a TTL in front of a slow price database.
Shows hits and misses, a stale read after a write WITHOUT invalidation, invalidate-on-write, and a
thundering herd: 50 concurrent misses on one cold key = 50 database reads. Simulated clock for TTLs."""
import threading, time

from helpers import SimClock


class PriceDB:
    """The source of truth (stands in for a remote database): slow on purpose, counts every read."""
    def __init__(self, delay=0.2):
        self.prices, self.reads, self.delay, self.lock = {"apple": 5}, 0, delay, threading.Lock()

    def read(self, sku):
        with self.lock:
            self.reads += 1
        time.sleep(self.delay)  # a slow query: the window in which a herd piles up
        return self.prices[sku]

    def write(self, sku, price):
        self.prices[sku] = price


class TTLCache:
    def __init__(self, ttl, clock):
        self.ttl, self.clock, self.data = ttl, clock, {}

    def get(self, key):  # None = absent or expired
        value, expires = self.data.get(key, (None, 0))
        return value if self.clock() < expires else None

    def set(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = (value, self.clock() + self.ttl)

    def delete(self, key):
        self.data.pop(key, None)


class PriceService:
    """Cache-aside: the application reads the cache, falls back to the DB on a miss, then fills the cache."""
    def __init__(self, db, cache, invalidate=True):
        self.db, self.cache, self.invalidate = db, cache, invalidate

    def get_price(self, sku):
        value = self.cache.get(sku)
        if value is None:  # miss: read the source of truth, then populate the cache for the next reader
            value = self.db.read(sku)
            self.cache.set(sku, value)
        return value

    def set_price(self, sku, price):
        self.db.write(sku, price)  # 1) write the database (the source of truth)
        if self.invalidate:
            self.cache.delete(sku)  # 2) invalidate-on-write: the next read misses and refetches


def herd(service, sku="apple", n=50):
    """n threads read one cold key at the same moment; returns (db reads, distinct values seen)."""
    start, seen, before = threading.Barrier(n), [], service.db.reads
    def reader():
        start.wait()
        seen.append(service.get_price(sku))
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=reader) for _ in range(n)]
    [t.start() for t in threads]
    [t.join() for t in threads]
    return service.db.reads - before, sorted(set(seen))


def main():
    db, clock = PriceDB(), SimClock()
    svc = PriceService(db, TTLCache(30, clock), invalidate=False)
    print("cache-aside  :", [svc.get_price("apple") for _ in range(3)], f"-> db reads {db.reads} (1 miss, 2 hits)")
    svc.set_price("apple", 7)  # no invalidation: the cache keeps 5 until its TTL (30 s) runs out
    for t in (0, 10, 29, 30):
        clock.t = t
        price = svc.get_price("apple")
        print(f"no invalidate: t={t:>2}s read {price}", "(STALE, db has 7)" if price != 7 else "(fresh)")
    svc.invalidate, clock.t = True, 100
    svc.set_price("apple", 9)
    print(f"invalidate   : t=100s write 9 -> read {svc.get_price('apple')} (fresh)")
    svc.cache.delete("apple")  # the key just expired ...
    reads, values = herd(svc)  # ... and 50 requests arrive together
    print(f"herd         : 50 concurrent reads of a cold key -> {reads} db reads, values {values}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

codeWalkthrough.title: TTL on read
codeWalkthrough.detail: `TTLCache.get` returns None once `clock() >= expires`, so expiry needs no background thread.

codeWalkthrough.title: Cache-aside miss path
codeWalkthrough.detail: `get_price`: miss -> `db.read` -> `cache.set`. The application, not the cache, talks to the database.

codeWalkthrough.title: Write order
codeWalkthrough.detail: `set_price` writes the database first, then deletes the cache key; deleting (not updating) is idempotent.

codeWalkthrough.title: The herd harness
codeWalkthrough.detail: `herd()` releases 50 threads with a Barrier so all of them check the cache before the first 0.2 s read returns.

equivalents: Same idea in Valkey: `SET price:apple 5 EX 30`, `GET`, `DEL` on write; `SET lock:apple me NX EX 5` lets one process load a cold key.
Same idea in Go: golang.org/x/sync/singleflight `Group.Do(key, fn)` — one execution in flight per key.
Same idea in memcache at Facebook: demand-filled look-aside cache, delete on write, leases against stale sets and herds.
inRealSystems: Facebook's memcache deletes (not updates) on write because deletes are idempotent, and leases cut a herd-prone key's peak DB rate from 17K/s to 1.3K/s.
Valkey's SET supports EX/PX TTLs and NX for a simple loader lock.
useWhen: Use cache-aside with a TTL for read-heavy data that may be briefly stale; add invalidation for user-visible writes and coalescing for hot keys; avoid caching data every reader must see fresh.
simulatorVsReal: The database is an in-process object with a 0.2 s sleep and the cache a dict; TTLs use a simulated clock. Valkey runs only in CI.
caution: A cache is not the source of truth: never write only to the cache, and never cache data across users or tenants with the same key.

title: Rate limiting: token bucket, per-client limits, 429 and Retry-After
description: An HTTP API with a token bucket per client answers 429 + Retry-After; a polite client waits as told, a naive one hammers, a quiet one is unaffected.
outcome: You can implement a token bucket, return 429 with a correct Retry-After, honour it in a client, and build a sliding-window limiter.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps).
overview: A per-client token bucket caps the average rate while allowing short bursts; 429 + Retry-After tells clients exactly when to come back.

glossary.meaning: Tokens refill at a fixed rate up to a burst size; each request spends one.
Response header: seconds to wait, or an HTTP date (RFC 9110).

concepts: Retry-After = ceil(time to next token), at least 1.

codeWalkthrough.title: Lazy refill
codeWalkthrough.detail: `tokens = min(burst, tokens + (now - last) * rate)`: no timer thread; tokens are computed when a request arrives.

codeWalkthrough.title: Wait until the next token
codeWalkthrough.detail: `(1 - tokens) / rate` seconds; the server sends `max(1, ceil(wait))` because delay-seconds is a whole number.

codeWalkthrough.title: Per-client limiter
codeWalkthrough.detail: `limiters.setdefault(client, ...)` creates one bucket per X-Client-Id on first use.

codeWalkthrough.title: Both Retry-After forms
codeWalkthrough.detail: `retry_after_seconds` accepts delay-seconds or an HTTP-date (parsed with email.utils).

equivalents: Same idea in Envoy: the local rate limit filter is a token bucket (max_tokens, tokens_per_fill, fill_interval), returns 429 and can add Retry-After in delay-seconds form.
Same idea in NGINX: limit_req (leaky bucket, rate + burst); rejected requests get 503 unless `limit_req_status 429`.
Same idea in Go: golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter, a token bucket with Allow, Reserve (returns the delay) and Wait.
Same idea in Valkey: INCR + EXPIRE per client per second (a fixed-window counter).
